title: When a Parabola is Tangent to the x-axis
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: For the parabola y = x^2 + bx + c, determine the condition on b and c under which the curve is tangent to the x-axis, and find the x-coordinate of the tangency point.

steps.title: Rephrase Tangency as a Double Root
steps.mathExpression: \text{tangent to } x\text{-axis} \iff x^2 + bx + c = 0 \text{ has exactly one real root}
steps.explanation: The parabola touches the axis without crossing it precisely when the quadratic equation has a single repeated solution where the vertex sits on y = 0.
steps.why: An upward-opening parabola crosses the axis twice for two real roots and never for none; the borderline grazing case is the double root.

steps.title: Set the Discriminant to Zero
steps.explanation: The quadratic formula shows the root count is governed by Delta; requiring a repeated root forces b^2 - 4c = 0, which pins c to b^2/4.
steps.why: sqrt(Delta) vanishes exactly when Delta does, collapsing the two formula roots (-b +/- sqrt(Delta))/2 into one.

steps.title: Locate the Tangency Point
steps.explanation: Under the tangency condition the quadratic becomes a perfect square, whose only zero is x = -b/2: this is both the vertex's x-coordinate and the point of contact with the axis.
steps.why: A perfect square is nonnegative and zero at exactly one input, so the vertex touches y = 0 there and nowhere else.

steps.title: Confirm Sufficiency
steps.explanation: Conversely, whenever c = b^2/4 the graph is the square-vertex form, which is everywhere nonnegative with a single contact point, proving the condition is both necessary and sufficient.
steps.why: The biconditional chain double-root <=> Delta = 0 <=> c = b^2/4 leaves no gap between necessity and sufficiency.
